hypothesis: The 56 ms spent before each ShuffleNetV2 job's doorbell is CPU work in job publication (hashing and address translation), not NPU time.
reference: vendor driver examples/vpm_run/vpm_run.c:2628, :2672-2704; vip_lite.h:600-601 (prepare once, flush input and invalidate output per run)

conditions.kind: host model plus board session records

conclusion: The board records place the time between the entry of the job publication and the counter start at 55.8-56.1 ms in all four jobs, the same at 492 and 852 MHz, so CPU work. Host model (checks/npu-job-cost.py, Unicorn, running the image's own constructor, SUBMIT and job callbacks) confirms the instruction counts; the hashing loop is about 98% of the instructions, which at 56 ms is about 1.1 ns per instruction, and the SUBMIT send of 368,016 instructions matches its measured 405 us at the same rate.
narrative: Run of board-session-20261025-12/port-3-3 (ShuffleNetV2, set 16 image): 56 ms of CPU time before each job's doorbell, 13-14 us between counter start and doorbell, about 17 us between interrupt and recorded completion. Before the change, unchanged() hashed the descriptors and coefficients (917,504 bytes) and the job command stream and scanned the 512 KiB command buffer's padding; a733_npu_memory_publish translated every page of every buffer with AT (1,065 translations) and cleaned or cleaned and invalidated the input, the 1,093,632-byte pool and the output, 19,520 cache lines. Job publication executed 49.6 M instructions with 920,616 bytes hashed.

hypothesis: Preparing once at open, plain register access, a two-write trigger and one event read at completion remove the fixed CPU cost of a job.
conclusion: Host-model counts and times (emulation) for the changed code are below. The first six rows come from checks/npu-job-cost.py on the set 16 image (before) and the changed branch image (after); the register-access counts include the two cycle-counter reads on each side. CLOSE hashes about 2 MB (about 110 M instructions, roughly 0.12 s at the board's rate) once per session. Against 11f00ff9, 42 of 68 default images change; code changes are limited to the images that link the NPU controller, adapter or convolution backend (accelerator composition, NPU board image, OS NPU profile, the five NPU models, the finite profiles); the other 26 differ only in build identity and debug information because include/a733_mmio.h gained the two DMB accessors.

The OS NPU profile and the NPU board image share the startup, controller and adapter and default to 852 MHz with plain register access, the two-write trigger and the single event read, but neither has had a board run of its own with these changes. The per-access split between bus and barrier cost is unmeasured; the doorbell timestamp of the next run measures the remaining two writes.

hypothesis: The clock-independent 1.85 ms of a ShuffleNetV2 inference is DRAM bandwidth, latency, NPU MMU table walks or the memory fabric clock.
prediction:
Set 16's two rates give T(f) = C/f + M with C ≈ 902,000 NPU cycles and
M ≈ 1.85 ms per ShuffleNetV2 inference. M does not shrink with the NPU clock.
Three measurements can attribute it:

- **Bandwidth counters.** The vendor's bandwidth profiling reads total read
  and write counters at `+0x040` and `+0x044` around a job, and on-chip
  buffer counters at `+0x5C0` and `+0x5D0`
  (`vip2/task/vip_drv_task_debug.c:270-277`); its hang dump also names read
  and write burst, request and outstanding-transaction counters at
  `+0x058`–`+0x060` and `+0x43C`–`+0x444` (`vip_drv_debug.c:551-560`).
  Logged beside the cycle counters, bytes moved divided by M gives the
  achieved DRAM bandwidth: near the bus limit points to DRAM bandwidth; far
  below it, with many outstanding reads, points to latency.
- **NPU MMU.** The tables map 4 KiB pages (785 for this graph). Mapping the
  same buffers with larger pages and comparing M isolates the cost of the
  NPU's table walks.
- **MBUS clock.** The image fixes MBUS at 600 MHz (`CCU+0x588`). A run with
  MBUS at another rate, or with the NPU clock fixed and the DRAM clock
  changed, shows whether M follows the memory fabric.
conclusion: Not run. Set 16's two rates (852 MHz 2.91 ms, 492 MHz 3.69 ms doorbell to interrupt) give T(f) = C/f + M with C about 902,000 NPU cycles and M about 1.85 ms; the three attributing measurements have not been performed.
narrative: Prediction recorded in the job-overhead design as three attributing measurements for the term M; none performed. MBUS is fixed at 600 MHz by the image (CCU+0x588). The NPU MMU tables map 4 KiB pages (785 for this graph).

hypothesis: The vendor operating point for the boards' speed bin is 852 MHz at 800 mV.
conclusion: Both boards are vf0400 and run at 852 MHz and 800 mV. Speed-bin codes vf0201, vf0400, vf0500 run 852 MHz; others are refused before any write.
narrative:
The vendor driver caps the rate at 1,008 MHz (npu-vfgear 0, vip_drv_device_platform.c:655-686), lists only table rows that have the bin's column (:736-790) and keeps the highest such row at or below the cap (:703-734).

| Speed bin, SID code | Vendor point |
| --- | --- |
| vf0000 (0x00), vf0200 (0x02), vf0401 (0x14) | 1,008 MHz at 960 mV |
| vf0300 (0x03), vf0501 (0x15) | 1,008 MHz at 900 mV |
| vf0201 (0x12), vf0400 (0x04), vf0500 (0x05) | 852 MHz at 800 mV |
| vf0100 (0x01), vf0101 (0x11), vf0600 (0x06) | no row |

Port 3-3 reads SID 0x0300624c = 0x496 and port 3-1 reads 0x495 (board-session-20261025-4/port-3-1/bb9-read): both are code 4, vf0400, whose column has no 1,008 MHz row. The vendor driver therefore runs both boards at 852 MHz with DCDC2 untouched at 800 mV.
